strengths: GQR is a simple, architecture-agnostic test-time refinement method that can combine heterogeneous single- and multi-vector retrievers without learning an explicit cross-space projection.
The evaluation covers nine vision/text retriever pairings, two benchmarks, multiple rank- and score-fusion baselines, a multimodal reranker, and several useful design ablations.

On ViDoRe 2, GQR consistently improves the primary retrievers and slightly outperforms tuned score fusion on average; the reported latency-quality and storage-quality tradeoffs are practically appealing.
The paper is generally well organized, and the central algorithm and motivation are easy to understand.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the method closely follows prior test-time query-representation optimization, principally replacing cross-encoder feedback with scores from another bi-encoder. Comparisons against prior query-optimization or stronger learned/dynamic fusion methods are missing, so it is unclear how much is gained beyond adapting an established mechanism.

The empirical gains are not uniformly compelling. On ViDoRe 1, average NDCG changes by approximately -0.1%, while the main ViDoRe 2 advantage over tuned min-max fusion is only about 0.2 NDCG when averaged across pairs. No confidence intervals, repeated splits, or significance tests establish that these differences are robust.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified: the paper does not clearly state test-set sample counts, how the remaining 90% is used after reserving 10% for development, split seeds, or sensitivity to per-subset hyperparameter tuning. Tuning separate GQR parameters for every subset also weakens the claimed practical generality.

Efficiency claims are difficult to reproduce and somewhat overstated. The index/search implementation, ANN settings, warm-up and timing details, variance, and included pipeline stages are omitted. Storage measures only raw FP16 embeddings rather than actual index memory, and the OCR/index-construction costs required by the complementary text retriever are excluded.

Important implementation details are ambiguous, including whether gradients flow through the p1 component of the consensus target, Adam settings, and normalization/scoring specifics for each model. The promised code link is absent, materially limiting reproducibility.

There are reporting inconsistencies: the stated memory reduction varies between approximately 24x and 28x, some latency/performance values differ across tables, and the text-only rows of the ViDoRe 1 Recall@5 table appear to duplicate NDCG values with the Avg and ArXivQA columns swapped.
Generality is demonstrated only within visual-document retrieval on closely related ViDoRe benchmarks, despite broad claims that GQR applies across retrieval architectures and settings.

strengths: GQR is a simple, architecture-agnostic test-time method that combines heterogeneous retrievers without training an additional fusion model or aligning their embedding dimensions.

The evaluation covers nine vision/text retriever pairs and includes rank- and score-fusion baselines, alternative objectives, candidate-pool variants, role reversal, and a multimodal reranker comparison.
On ViDoRe 2, GQR improves NDCG@5 across all nine tested pairs, with an average relative gain of 3.9%, and provides attractive measured latency-quality tradeoffs.
The paper is generally clear, and the motivation around the substantial index cost of late-interaction visual retrievers is practically relevant.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the method closely follows prior test-time query-representation optimization and pseudo-relevance-feedback approaches, primarily replacing a cross-encoder teacher with another bi-encoder and applying the idea to multimodal retrieval. Describing this as representation-level fusion overstates the contribution because the complementary model supplies only document scores.

The empirical gains are modest and concentrated on ViDoRe 2. On ViDoRe 1, average NDCG@5 slightly decreases, and many individual configurations or subsets regress. Thus, claims of consistent improvement and broad effectiveness are stronger than the evidence supports.

No uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported. This is important because several headline differences from tuned score fusion are small: 62.3 versus 62.1 average NDCG@5, with GQR also losing to a tuned baseline on some subsets.

The evaluation tunes learning rate and iteration count on an in-domain development portion separately for every dataset subset, but does not examine sensitivity, robustness to a shared configuration, or transfer to unseen domains. The setup may therefore overstate practical generalization and makes the comparison sensitive to tuning protocol.

The efficiency claims are incomplete. Storage figures primarily count embedding floats and omit model weights, OCR-derived text storage, and broader system costs; latency is measured on one A100 without sufficient details about indexing backend, batching, warm-up, variance, or whether all ingestion and retrieval stages are treated consistently.

The reranker comparison is narrow and not fully matched: GQR uses a union of candidates from two independently searched indices, whereas the reranker receives candidates from only the primary retriever. Only one reranker is considered, and the stronger top-10 reranking configuration generally outperforms GQR in quality.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including whether gradients are propagated through or detached from the consensus target, exactly how hyperparameters are selected for each model pair, and the ANN/index configuration. The promised code link is also absent in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.

The paper lacks analysis explaining when and why refinement helps or hurts—for example, results broken down by overlap, complementarity, modality dependence, or query type. Consequently, the main mechanism and its likely behavior beyond these benchmarks remain insufficiently established.

strengths: GQR is a clear and practically relevant contribution: it adapts test-time query optimization to hybrid multimodal retrieval while remaining architecture-agnostic and requiring no retriever retraining.

The empirical study is broad within the target setting, covering three vision retrievers, three complementary text retrievers, nine model pairings, two ViDoRe benchmark versions, and eight rank- or score-fusion baselines.

Results on the more challenging ViDoRe 2 benchmark are consistent: GQR improves average NDCG@5 for all nine model pairs and generally outperforms tuned hybrid-fusion baselines. The reported gains are especially useful for the weaker Jina vision retriever.

The latency and per-document storage analysis demonstrates attractive practical tradeoffs. In particular, Colnomic plus GQR approximately matches or exceeds the substantially larger Llama-Nemo system while using much less index memory and lower query latency.

The paper includes useful analyses of candidate-pool construction, an additional search pass, alternative loss functions, reversed retriever roles, recall, and comparison with a multimodal reranker. The method and hyperparameter grids are described clearly.
weaknesses: The improvements are modest overall, and the paper reports neither confidence intervals nor significance tests. This matters because evaluation sets are divided by subset, 10% is used for development, and several reported differences are below one NDCG point.

GQR receives substantially more hyperparameter selection than some baselines: its learning rate and iteration count are tuned separately for every dataset subset, while standard fusion variants mostly tune a single weight. Hyperparameter sensitivity, a shared global configuration, and performance under limited or out-of-domain development data are not evaluated.

The reranker comparison is not fully controlled. GQR uses the union of two top-10 lists, potentially containing 20 candidates, whereas the highlighted reranker pipelines rerank only 5 or 10 candidates from one primary retriever. Thus the quality and Pareto comparisons partly reflect different candidate generators and budgets.

The efficiency claims focus on query latency and index bytes per document but omit important deployment costs, including keeping and executing a second multi-billion-parameter encoder, OCR/Docling preprocessing, model-weight memory, and index-building time. The broad claim of deployment efficiency should therefore be qualified.

Evidence is concentrated on one benchmark family: ViDoRe 1 is saturated and shows essentially no average NDCG improvement, leaving ViDoRe 2 as the main positive result. Evaluation on another collection, corpus scale, or retrieval domain would strengthen generality.

The paper does not cleanly isolate refinement from candidate-pool expansion using a no-optimization baseline that unions both retrievers' candidates and ranks them solely with the primary model. Score-fusion baselines are informative but do not answer this exact question.

There are minor presentation and reproducibility issues, including inconsistent retriever/distribution notation in Figure 4, an incomplete code-release sentence in the abstract, and insufficient detail about latency timing boundaries and variability.

strengths: GQR is a clear, technically plausible test-time method: it uses a complementary retriever’s score distribution to optimize the primary retriever’s query representation without retraining either model.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this problem, covering three ViDoRe generations, multiple primary and complementary retrievers, tuned and zero-shot settings, NDCG and recall, conventional hybrid baselines, and a multimodal reranker.
The empirical pattern is consistent: GQR improves every model pair on average, transfers zero-shot to ViDoRe 3, and generally performs more robustly than rank- or score-level fusion.

The efficiency analysis is practically relevant and includes latency breakdowns, storage estimates, Pareto comparisons, and several useful design ablations. The Colnomic-based variants offer compelling quality-efficiency tradeoffs relative to Llama-Nemo.

The manuscript is well organized and the method, implementation choices, and selected hyperparameters are documented in substantial detail. weaknesses: The advantage over the strongest tuned score-fusion baseline is small: on ViDoRe 2, GQR averages 62.3 NDCG@5 versus 62.1 for tuned min-max fusion, and on ViDoRe 3 the relative gains are 2.89% versus 2.66%. No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or variability across query splits are reported, so the central superiority claim is not decisively established.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. Test-time query-embedding optimization from relevance feedback is established in prior work; the main change is replacing a cross-encoder teacher with a complementary bi-encoder and using a consensus distribution. Direct experimental comparisons to adapted prior query-refinement methods are missing.

The baseline set is limited to fixed global rank/score fusion. Stronger alternatives—such as query-dependent fusion, learned fusion on the same development data, or equally budgeted optimization/calibration baselines—would better test whether representation-space optimization itself is responsible for the gain.

The tuning and evaluation protocol needs greater clarity. The paper says 10% of each subset is reserved for tuning but does not explicitly state whether all reported ViDoRe 1/2 results exclude those queries, nor does it report sensitivity to the random split. Per-subset tuning over many learning-rate/step combinations may overfit small development sets.

Efficiency claims require qualification. The reported memory advantage concerns document-index storage rather than total serving memory, despite GQR requiring two multi-billion-parameter encoders and two indexes. Latency is measured on one A100 using 100 sampled queries without variance, batching/concurrency analysis, or sufficiently detailed index-search configuration.

The claimed architecture-agnostic generality is supported only within visual-document retrieval and a limited family of dense/late-interaction models. Evaluation on text retrieval, other modality pairings, larger candidate pools/corpora, and more realistic noisy OCR would strengthen this claim.

The paper occasionally overstates consistency: ViDoRe 3 includes small negative per-subset changes, and ViDoRe 1 is essentially neutral rather than beneficial. The lack of a dedicated limitations discussion also leaves issues such as off-manifold query updates and hyperparameter instability underexplored.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, architecture-agnostic test-time method for incorporating a complementary retriever’s signal by optimizing the primary query representation. The empirical study covers three ViDoRe benchmark generations, several primary/complementary model pairings, tuned and zero-shot settings, NDCG and recall, and multiple conventional hybrid-retrieval baselines.

The efficiency analysis is practically relevant: the results suggest that combining a moderate-size vision retriever with a text retriever can approach a much more storage-intensive late-interaction model at substantially lower measured latency and index memory.

The appendices contain useful design studies covering candidate construction, an additional index search, alternative objectives, swapped model roles, hyperparameter sensitivity, and comparison with a multimodal reranker.
weaknesses: The incremental benefit attributable specifically to GQR is weak. On ViDoRe 2, GQR obtains 62.3 average NDCG@5 versus 62.1 for tuned min-max score fusion; on ViDoRe 3, the reported relative gains are 2.89% versus 2.66%. No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or per-query uncertainty analyses establish that these small differences are reliable.

Novelty is limited by substantial prior work on test-time query-representation optimization and relevance feedback. The main conceptual change is replacing a cross-encoder teacher with another bi-encoder and applying the idea to multimodal retrieval. The paper does not sharply isolate which contribution goes beyond this substitution.

The tuned evaluation risks overfitting: hyperparameters are selected separately for every dataset subset and model pair using only a 10% development split, over a sizable search space. Sample counts, split variability, repeated-seed results, and sensitivity to development-set selection are not reported. The ViDoRe 3 result helps, but provides only one zero-shot transfer setting and only a very small advantage over tuned score fusion.

The reranker comparison is not fully controlled. GQR uses the union of top-10 results from two retrievers, potentially providing up to 20 candidates, whereas the described reranking pipelines operate on the primary retriever’s top-k results. Candidate recall and the cost of obtaining equivalent candidate pools should be matched before drawing strong Pareto conclusions.

The efficiency claims omit important deployment costs. The paper reports index storage per document but not the additional model weights or runtime GPU memory required to keep two multi-billion-parameter encoders available. Latency methodology also lacks details such as index size and implementation, warm-up, batching, variance, and whether operations were synchronized; measurements from one A100 therefore provide limited evidence of general scalability.

The optimization definition is reproducibly ambiguous: the consensus distribution contains the primary distribution and therefore depends on the optimized query, but the paper does not state whether gradients are stopped through this target. Differentiating through it versus detaching it yields different objectives and updates.

Because the final method only reorders a small initial candidate union and an additional full-index search provides no gain, the contribution is closer to candidate-set reranking than a broadly validated retrieval method. Evaluation at larger corpus sizes and larger K values is needed to support the real-world scalability framing.

strengths: GQR is a clear and practically relevant test-time method: it uses a complementary retriever to refine the primary retriever's query representation without additional training and supports both single- and multi-vector architectures.

The evaluation is broad, covering three visual-document-retrieval benchmarks, multiple modern vision and text retrievers, nine model pairings on ViDoRe 1/2, and a genuinely useful zero-shot transfer experiment on ViDoRe 3.

Results are consistently positive on the less-saturated ViDoRe 2 and ViDoRe 3 benchmarks. GQR improves every model-pair average and generally outperforms rank- and score-level fusion, including tuned variants.

The efficiency analysis is compelling: some GQR configurations approach or exceed the strongest large-representation retriever while substantially reducing latency and index storage. The comparison with a multimodal reranker further supports the practical motivation.

The paper includes useful investigations of learning rate and optimization steps, candidate-pool construction, an additional index-search pass, alternative losses, swapped retriever roles, and Recall@5 results. The presentation is generally clear and well organized.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but incremental relative to prior test-time query optimization and pseudo-relevance-feedback methods. The principal change is replacing a strong reranker or cross-encoder signal with another bi-encoder and optimizing toward a consensus distribution; the paper could distinguish its technical contribution more sharply from this literature.

The advantage over the strongest score-fusion baseline is fairly small. On zero-shot ViDoRe 3, GQR improves the primary model by 2.89% versus 2.66% for min-max score aggregation, and on tuned ViDoRe 2 its average NDCG@5 is 62.3 versus 62.1. No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or query-level uncertainty estimates establish that these differences are reliable.

The differentiation semantics of the objective are insufficiently explicit. Because the consensus target contains the primary distribution and therefore depends on the optimized query embedding, it matters whether gradients flow through that target or it is detached; this materially changes the objective and should be specified for reproducibility.

The tuned experiments select learning rate and step count separately for every dataset subset and model pair using 10% development splits. This extensive tuning may favor GQR, while the paper does not report split sizes, variability across splits, or a less highly specialized shared-configuration result on ViDoRe 2.

Some efficiency and reranker comparisons need tighter controls. GQR searches two indexes and uses the union of two top-K lists, potentially providing up to twice as many candidates as a primary-only top-K reranker. Latency is reported on one A100 without enough detail about corpus sizes, index/search implementation, batching, warm-up, or variance to extrapolate confidently to large production collections.

Reproducibility is only moderate despite the promised code release: important implementation details such as gradient detachment, score precision, stopping behavior, optimizer-state handling, exact indexing configuration, and complete timing methodology are not fully documented.
